title: Zoos
resolution: Resolved: Zoos do more good than harm.
summary: Zoos say they protect endangered species and teach visitors to care about wildlife. Critics say captivity harms many animals and the benefits are overstated. Which weighs more?

background.p: Modern accredited zoos describe their missions as conservation, education, research and animal welfare. Many take part in cooperative breeding programs for threatened species and fund field conservation. Some species, such as the California condor and the Arabian oryx, survived in part because of breeding in zoos and similar facilities, and were later returned to the wild.

Evidence on zoos' effects on visitors is mixed. A 2019 review in *Frontiers in Psychology* (Godinez and Fernandez) found that interactive programs and naturalistic exhibits improve learning and attitudes, and that visitors take more conservation actions on site, but that few studies compare zoo visitors with non-visitors, so the effect on behavior after leaving is largely unknown. Visitors who see animals pacing or showing other repetitive behaviors rate the animals' welfare and their own visit lower.
Standards vary widely: accredited zoos follow detailed welfare rules, while some roadside attractions do not. The resolution asks about zoos in general, so debaters should say which zoos they mean.

disputed.q: Do zoo visits change how people treat wildlife?
positions: Studies find visitors learn and take conservation actions at the zoo, especially through interactive programs.
Reviews note few studies follow visitors afterward or compare them with non-visitors, so lasting effects are uncertain.

terms.def: A zoo that meets an association's standards for animal care, safety and conservation.
A cooperative breeding program among zoos to keep a healthy captive population of a threatened species.
Repetitive behavior with no clear purpose, such as pacing, often seen as a sign of poor welfare.
Releasing animals bred in captivity back into the wild.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Good zoos save species, fund conservation and help people care about wildlife.

args.warrant: When wild populations collapse, a carefully managed captive population can keep a species alive and supply animals for reintroduction.
args.evidence: Recoveries of the California condor and Arabian oryx; cooperative breeding program records.
args.response: The negative answers that only a small share of zoo animals belong to threatened species in such programs.

args.claim: Zoos fund and support conservation in the wild.
args.warrant: Ticket sales and donations pay for field researchers, habitat protection and anti-poaching work that wouldn't otherwise be funded.
args.evidence: Zoo association reports on field conservation spending; partnerships with wildlife agencies.
args.response: The negative replies that the same money could go straight to habitat protection without keeping animals in captivity.

args.claim: Zoos teach people to value wildlife.
args.warrant: Seeing a living animal creates a connection that a screen can't, especially for children who will never see one in the wild.
args.evidence: Godinez and Fernandez (2019) on learning from interactive programs and naturalistic exhibits.
args.response: The negative answers that the same review found little evidence of lasting behavior change after visitors leave.

args.claim: Zoos advance science that helps wild animals.
args.warrant: Research on animal health, reproduction and behavior in zoos helps veterinarians and field biologists protect wild populations.
args.evidence: Studies published by zoo researchers; veterinary advances from zoo medicine.
args.response: The negative argues that animals in captivity may behave differently, limiting what research shows about the wild.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Captivity harms many animals, and the benefits zoos claim are smaller than they appear.

args.claim: Captivity can harm animal welfare, especially for some species.
args.warrant: Wide-ranging, intelligent or social animals such as elephants, great apes and large carnivores may suffer in limited spaces, shown by pacing and other stereotypic behaviors.
args.evidence: Welfare research on elephants and carnivores in captivity; Godinez and Fernandez on visitor reactions to stereotypic behavior.
args.response: The affirmative answers that modern accredited zoos have redesigned habitats and some have stopped keeping species that do poorly.

args.claim: Most zoo animals aren't part of conservation programs.
args.warrant: If the main justification is saving species, keeping many animals that aren't endangered or ever released is hard to justify.
args.evidence: Inventories of zoo collections compared with threatened-species lists.
args.response: The affirmative replies that non-endangered animals still serve education and fundraising that support conservation.

args.warrant: If visits don't change behavior after people leave, a key benefit is overstated.
args.evidence: The 2019 review's finding that the zoo's effect beyond its walls is largely unknown.
args.response: The affirmative argues that the absence of long-term studies isn't evidence of no effect.

args.warrant: Species survive long-term only if their habitats survive; money and attention spent on captive collections may be better spent protecting wild places.
args.evidence: Conservation research on habitat loss as a leading threat to species.
args.response: The affirmative replies that zoos already fund habitat work, and captive populations are insurance when habitats fail.

strawmen.strawman: Zoo supporters think animals exist for our entertainment.
strawmen.why: Supporters emphasize conservation, research and education, and accredited zoos follow welfare standards.
strawmen.steelman: Good zoos keep endangered species alive, fund field conservation and help people, especially children, care about wildlife.

strawmen.strawman: Zoo critics want every animal set free in the wild tomorrow.
strawmen.why: Many critics favor sanctuaries, phasing out certain species and funding habitats, not sudden release.
strawmen.steelman: Captivity harms many animals, most zoo animals aren't in conservation programs, and the education benefits are poorly supported; habitat protection does more good.

weak.arg: Animals in zoos are happier because they get free food.
weak.why: Welfare research shows needs beyond food; this is easy to refute.

weak.arg: Zoos are just prisons for animals.
weak.why: A slogan; it skips the conservation evidence your opponent will raise.

aff: What share of zoo animals belong to endangered-species programs?
Which species do poorly in captivity?
What does research show about visitors' behavior after they leave?
neg: How did the California condor survive?
Should accredited zoos and roadside attractions be judged the same way?
Where would the animals in zoos go?
